extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; historians of print culture; general readers interested in early newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of the development and forms of newspaper advertising in seventeenth-century England, illustrated with many period examples (lost/stolen notices, service schedules, publisher notices, protests, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include places of abode / addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the addresses or places of abode of shops, practitioners, and sellers so the notice is practically useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes Houghton 'published ... the addresses of some of the principal shops, but also a list of the residences of the leading doctors.' He even offers: 'If desired I'll set down the places of abode.' Providing addresses made the paper 'more permanently useful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish lists of practitioners' residences (professional directories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile and publish lists of residences/addresses of professionals (e.g., doctors) as part of advertising material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'we gather that in June 1694 there were 93 doctors in and about London' with named residences (e.g., 'Dr Hans Sloane lived at Montague House'). Such lists functioned as directories and advertising aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, graphic local detail to illuminate context
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill notices and columns with graphic details that 'throw a clear and effective light' on contemporary life, making adverts informative and evocative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises papers as 'full of graphic details' that give vivid pictures (e.g., winter road conditions, domestic scenes, auctions) — adverts that include concrete, local colour engage readers and document the times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use advertisements to publish contradictions, retractions, and defensive notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish adverts to contradict rumours, deny false reports, or defend reputation (a public protest by the author/subject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 1647 paragraph: a gentleman requests that 'all that are credulous ... may be assured that it's all fabulous' regarding a devil story; and Lilly's full advertisement protesting that he 'never wrote any such thing' about predicting fires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed identifying descriptions in lost/stolen/property notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe lost/stolen animals and goods with specific physical markers (colour, markings, age, scars, tack, tail, gait) to enable identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: stolen horses described with markings ('bay-bald Gelding with three white feet, ... Marked with R. F.'), a 'Small black NAG' described in exhaustive detail (saddle, girths, tail, hair worn off at a spot 'as broad as a twelvepence'). Such precision aids recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: State reward amounts and return instructions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the monetary reward and precise instructions for where or to whom to report or return found items or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'they shall have 20s. for each Horse'; notices instructing to bring tidings 'to Mr Bullen at Bronifield, or to Mr Newman ...' or 'leave word with Mr Samuel Merne ... and they shall be thankfully rewarded.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise service schedules, prices, and operating instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish days, times, prices (fees), and operational conditions for services (e.g., postmasters' horse hire and stage arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postmasters' advertisement gives specific schedule: 'upon every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday Morning, betwixt Six and ten of the Clock' and price 'Threepence the Mile, without the charge of a Guide', plus operational rules about stages and notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use advertisements to promote forthcoming publications and sales locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Announce new books/works with title information and seller/purchase location so readers know where to obtain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Milton's work listed with title and 'Sold by Liveivel Chapman, at the Crown in Pope's Head Alley' and other publisher notices; simple bibliographic-advertisements were common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish errata and corrections publicly for printed works
rubrics_metrics.description: Print errata/corrections and request that certain 'faults may be amended' as part of advertising or publisher notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Weekly Account example prints an errata note: 'Wherein, by reason of the Printer's haste, the Errata not coming in time, it is desired that the following faults may be amended...' demonstrating that corrections were communicated via the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use advertisements to ventilate grievances and influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ adverts to air complaints, political positions, or to influence public sentiment (meetings, claims to estates, political barometers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes that advertisements served as a 'capital barometer of the state of feeling among political men' (e.g., meetings to secure sequestered estates, parliamentary disclaimers), and that publications advertised to sway opinion at critical junctures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise for missing persons or news of absent relatives with reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek news of missing people (e.g., soldiers, apprentices) by publishing notices describing the person and offering a reward for certainty of death or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a notice about 'George Weale, a Cornish youth ... went secretly ... is conceived to have engaged ... and is either dead or slain ... If any person can give notice ... he shall have twenty shillings for his pains.'

rubrics_metrics.name: List detailed inventories of lost personal baggage and require return to named agent
rubrics_metrics.description: When personal luggage is lost, include an itemised inventory of contents and direct return to a named person or office for reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The leather portmanteau notice enumerates contents ('a suit of Camolet Holland, with two little laces ... eight pair of white Gloves ... twenty yards of skie-colourd Ribbon ...') and instructs to leave word with 'Mr Samuel Merne' for reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emotive or satirical tone and rhetorical devices in notices to attract attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ rhetorical flourishes (satire, mock-exasperation, patriotic ridicule) in adverts to draw interest or shame intended targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the King's dog notices adopt a mocking tone ('Will they never leave robbing His Majesty? must he not keep a Dog?') and other adverts use lively phrases and character sketches to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise practical performance promises and service assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: State assurances about service performance, delivery times, and what customers can expect (e.g., 'will have all such set days so many Horses ... in readiness ... to furnish the Riders ... with expedition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postmasters guarantee stage arrangements and promptness ('ingaging at the first Stage ... for the safe delivery of the same to the next immediate Stage'), showing adverts served as service contracts/assurances.
